messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir believed his hands were his most reliable asset. For fifteen years, they had been steady, creative, and sure, snipping and styling in his bustling salon, a place filled with the scent of shampoo and the easy chatter of his clients. That sense of reliability shattered nine months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. One moment he was laughing with a longtime customer, scissors in hand; the next, a crushing weight descended on his chest, a brutal, searing pain that stole his breath and sent a terrifying ache down his left arm. He remembers the metallic taste in his mouth, the smell of antiseptic on the paramedic’s gloves, and the disorienting blur of ceiling tiles as he was wheeled through the emergency room. He had survived a sudden, severe cardiac event that the doctors called a fluke for a man of 38. But while his heart had physically healed, his sense of safety had not.

In the weeks that followed, Amir tried to reclaim his old life, but it was as if the memory of the event had lodged itself in his body. At first, it was the nightmares, vivid and chaotic, that left him waking in a tangle of sweat-soaked sheets. Even when he couldn't recall the specifics of the dream, a residue of pure dread would cling to him all morning, making the simple act of getting out of bed feel monumental. Then came the phantom sensations. Standing at his station, the clean, sharp smell of a particular styling product would suddenly be replaced by the sterile, chemical scent of the ICU, a smell so real he would gag. With the scent came a ghostly echo of the pain, a hot clenching in his chest that would make him drop his comb and brace himself against the counter, convinced it was happening all over again. Sometimes, there was no trigger at all; just a sudden, overwhelming wave of horror that would rise in his throat while he was driving or making dinner, an intense emotion completely untethered to any image or thought.

These experiences became his secret shame. He was certain he was going crazy, that his mind had broken in some fundamental way. He began to see his own body as an enemy, a traitor that was constantly sounding a false alarm. He felt perpetually on edge, his shoulders tight and his jaw clenched, as if waiting for the next blow. A routine dental appointment a few months ago became an ordeal; the simple act of reclining in the chair and having a medical professional lean over him sent his heart into a frantic, hammering rhythm. He felt dizzy, his palms grew slick with sweat, and he had to pretend to have a coughing fit just to get them to stop. He never went back to have the filling completed. His mother, trying to be helpful, had put together a small album of photos from his time in the hospital, showing him surrounded by family. The sight of his own pale face, tubes taped to his skin, sent such a jolt of fear through him that he had to shove the book in a drawer, unable to look at it again.

The salon, once his sanctuary, was now a minefield. The constant physical tension made the long hours on his feet exhausting, and he found himself watching his own reflection in the mirror, scrutinizing his complexion, monitoring his breathing. He had come to believe that any strong emotion—even a flash of anger at a rude driver or a wave of sadness watching a film—was dangerous, a potential trigger for another attack. He began cancelling last-minute appointments, telling clients he wasn't feeling well, which was technically true. The loss of income was worrying, but the fear of collapsing in front of a client was worse. He felt utterly alone with this, convinced that he could no longer trust the very body he lived in. It was after a particularly bad panic attack during a routine blood pressure check at a pharmacy kiosk—an attack that left him breathless and shaking on a public bench—that Amir finally made a call to seek help. He didn't know if he could ever feel normal again, but he knew he could not continue to live as a prisoner in his own skin, perpetually waiting for a catastrophe that had already happened.
